title: Student ML Driving Lab: teaching kit

objectives.text: Explain what the network observes and outputs, and distinguish its learned commands (steering, target speed) from the automatic pedals and gears.
Build a labelled dataset and justify splitting whole driving episodes (never neighbouring frames) and keeping labels consistent.
Trace one minibatch update (forward pass, weighted error, backpropagated gradient, Adam step) and verify a gradient numerically.
Compare a learned policy with hand-written rules and an expert on matched starts, separating completed sections from failures.
Design and interpret retrain-from-scratch input-removal experiments, recognising that correlated inputs carry shared information.
Distinguish validation error on the training distribution from error on a deliberately different (stress) distribution.
Explain why training loss can keep falling while closed-loop driving does not improve, using success-versus-update curves across seeds.
Diagnose under- and over-fitting from train and validation curves and respond with more data, regularisation, early stopping or a different model class.
Explain covariate shift and compare expert-only demonstrations with on-policy aggregation (DAgger) using a matched control.
Locate where a failed drive first departs from the expert, test whether the expert could recover from that state, and read permutation importance with its caveats.
Explain why test data must stay unseen until the recipe is frozen, and recognise contamination.
Predict and measure the effect of noise, delay and reduced grip, and explain why measuring robustness is not the same as learning it.
Report uncertainty correctly: choose the unit of replication (training seed, fixed section, independent start), use the matching interval, and avoid over-reading small samples.
State a hypothesis before running, change one factor, report the evidence and state the limits of the conclusion.
Contrast imitation with reinforcement learning: what each is given (expert labels or a reward), who produces the experience it learns from, and what each costs in driving steps.
Judge a learner by a whole-task test (a full lap) at every stage of training rather than by one good run, and explain how a reward that leaves something out can be satisfied in an unintended way.

misconceptions.text: Lower loss means the car will drive better.
misconceptions.remedy: Module 2 and Module 6 plot closed-loop success beside the loss: the loss can fall by half while success is flat or erratic. Offline error is measured on recorded states; driving compounds small errors.

misconceptions.text: Any gap between training and validation loss is overfitting.
misconceptions.remedy: Module 2 shows three curves. Validation is drawn from the same episodes-and-starts distribution as training; the stress curve is a different distribution. A gap can mean overfitting or distribution shift; check what each set contains first.

misconceptions.text: More training updates always help.
misconceptions.remedy: Module 6 early stopping and the success-versus-update curve: validation loss can rise while training loss falls, and driving success can drop between checkpoints.

misconceptions.text: A bigger network is always better.
misconceptions.remedy: Module 6 capacity sweep on a tiny dataset: a larger network fits the training rows more closely and generalises no better.

misconceptions.text: Three successes in three trials means the policy is reliable.
misconceptions.remedy: Wilson intervals (independent starts only) show 3/3 is compatible with a true success rate near 44%. Use more trials and report the interval.

misconceptions.text: If removing an input changes nothing, the input is unimportant.
misconceptions.remedy: Module 5: heading is also encoded in the road previews. Absence of a measured effect with ten seeds is not proof of irrelevance.

misconceptions.text: Permutation importance shows what causes the decision.
misconceptions.remedy: Module 8: it measures how much the loss worsens when an input is scrambled across examples. Correlated inputs share credit, and scrambling can create unrealistic combinations.

misconceptions.text: DAgger always beats copying the expert.
misconceptions.remedy: Module 7 compares four recipes with equal label and update budgets. Outcomes depend on coverage and on the seed; the staged expert-only control isolates what on-policy data adds.

misconceptions.text: The test set can be used to tune as long as I never train on it.
misconceptions.remedy: Module 9: every look at test results that influences a choice makes the result exploratory. Freeze the recipe, then test once.

misconceptions.text: One training run shows how a recipe behaves.
misconceptions.remedy: Modules 5, 6 and 7 repeat each recipe over seeds: identical recipes differ by many sections between seeds.

misconceptions.text: Testing under noise makes the model robust.
misconceptions.remedy: Module 10 only measures a shift the model never trained for. Robustness would have to be learned (for example by training with noise) and then measured again.

misconceptions.text: The network outputs throttle, brake and gear directly.
misconceptions.remedy: Module 1: the network outputs steering and a target speed; ordinary controllers turn that into pedals and gears.

misconceptions.text: Neighbouring frames are independent examples.
misconceptions.remedy: Module 2: frames from one drive are almost identical. Splitting frames at random leaks information; split whole episodes, and never reuse the same start across splits.

misconceptions.text: If the car crashed, the last steering command caused it.
misconceptions.remedy: Module 8: the expert-recovery test shows from which earlier state the expert could still finish. The mistake usually happens earlier than the crash.

misconceptions.text: The expert is perfect, so imitation can match it exactly.
misconceptions.remedy: The expert is a heuristic: about 2% of typical starts (the fast, off-centre ones) trip the lateral-acceleration limit at the first steps. A learner cannot exceed its labels.

misconceptions.text: Every trial in a pool is an independent sample, so pooled trials give a confidence interval.
misconceptions.remedy: Trials inside one fixed section share a track and start family. Sections (or seeds) are the unit of replication; pooled Wilson intervals are only valid for independent random starts.

misconceptions.text: A training step moves every weight by exactly the learning rate times its gradient.
misconceptions.remedy: Module 3 shows the real Adam update: running averages of the gradient and of its square rescale each weight's step, so weights with the same gradient can move by different amounts and the very first steps are normalised by bias correction.

misconceptions.text: Changing several settings at once finds the best recipe faster.
misconceptions.remedy: Module 11: when two factors change together, any difference has two possible causes. Change exactly one factor, keep starts, seeds and budgets matched, and state the prediction before running.

misconceptions.text: Covariate shift is the same problem as test-set leakage.
misconceptions.remedy: Leakage is a bookkeeping error: evaluation information reaches training (Module 9). Covariate shift belongs to the method: the learner's own mistakes change which states it sees, so even perfectly clean data leaves gaps (Module 7).

misconceptions.text: Reinforcement learning is just imitation learning under another name, or a cheaper version of it.
misconceptions.remedy: Module 12 trains both on the same circuit with the same network. Imitation is given an expert's labels and needs a few hundred to a few thousand driving steps; reinforcement is given only a reward and needs tens of thousands before the car stays on the lap. Which costs less depends on whether you have an expert or a simulator you can crash freely.

misconceptions.text: If the car completes the lap, or its reward score is high, it drives the way we want.
misconceptions.remedy: A reward measures only what it contains. Without a steering-smoothness term every reinforcement car got round the lap while flicking its steering every 0.1 s: the score was fine and the driving was not. Choose the reward without that term in Module 12 and compare the steering-movement column.

misconceptions.text: The crash rate during training is the crash rate of the finished car.
misconceptions.remedy: Reinforcement learning explores by adding random noise to its commands while it trains, and that noise causes crashes the finished car would not make. The lap tests in Module 12 switch the noise off, which is why a noticeable share of training drives can still end in a crash while the lap test succeeds.

quiz.prompt: What does the neural network output?

choices.text: Steering and a target speed
choices.why: Ordinary controllers turn the target speed into throttle, brake and gear.

choices.text: Throttle, brake and gear directly
choices.why: Pedals and gears are produced by fixed rules, not learned.

choices.text: A reward for avoiding the wall
choices.why: In modules 1 to 11 the network is trained from expert labels, not a reward. Module 12 adds a reinforcement learner that does use a reward, but its network still outputs steering and a target speed.

quiz.prompt: Why are whole driving episodes assigned to either training or validation?

choices.text: Neighbouring frames are almost identical, so random frame splits leak information
choices.why: Validation then measures memory of near-duplicates rather than generalisation.

choices.text: Validation sets must be tiny
choices.why: Size is not the issue; independence is.

choices.text: It makes the loss curve smoother
choices.why: Smoothness is incidental; leakage is the problem.

quiz.prompt: In one Adam update, the change to a weight is

choices.text: Based on running averages of the gradient, so it is not simply minus the learning rate times the gradient
choices.why: Adam rescales by corrected first and second gradient moments.

choices.text: Exactly minus the learning rate times the gradient
choices.why: That is plain gradient descent, not Adam.

choices.text: Random noise added to the old weight
choices.why: The update is deterministic given the batch and the moment history.

quiz.prompt: Training loss 0.014, validation loss 0.016, recovery-stress loss 0.078. What does the stress gap mostly show?

choices.text: The stress states come from a different distribution than the training and validation states
choices.why: Validation matches training; stress deliberately does not, so a high stress loss measures coverage, not overfitting.

choices.text: The model has overfitted to the validation set
choices.why: Validation and training agree closely, which argues against overfitting.

choices.text: The optimiser has a bug
choices.why: Nothing here points to an optimiser fault.

quiz.prompt: The loss falls at every checkpoint, but closed-loop success bounces up and down. The best explanation is that

choices.text: Loss averages action error over recorded states, while driving compounds small errors into states the data may not cover
choices.why: Closed-loop success depends on what happens after the first mistake.

choices.text: The loss function is wrong
choices.why: The same loss measures what it is defined to measure; it simply is not task success.

choices.text: Success is random noise in the animation
choices.why: Every success count comes from an actual simulated drive.

quiz.prompt: Training loss is near zero while validation loss keeps rising. Which response fits?

choices.text: More data, weight decay, early stopping or a smaller network
choices.why: All reduce the gap between memorising the training rows and generalising.

choices.text: Train for many more updates
choices.why: Longer training deepens the memorisation.

choices.text: Use a larger network
choices.why: More capacity makes memorisation easier.

quiz.prompt: In imitation learning, covariate shift means

choices.text: The learner visits states that the expert's demonstrations never covered
choices.why: Its own small mistakes move it off the expert's distribution, where labels are missing.

choices.text: The expert changes its labelling rule over time
choices.why: The expert is a fixed function of the state.

choices.text: Test labels leak into the training data
choices.why: That is evaluation leakage, a different problem.

quiz.prompt: Why does the coverage lab include a staged expert-only control next to DAgger?

choices.text: It matches DAgger's schedule, budget and start distribution, so the difference isolates who chooses the visited states
choices.why: Without a matched control, differences could come from timing or start distribution.

choices.text: Because DAgger always wins
choices.why: Results depend on coverage and seed; the lab makes no such claim.

choices.text: To use fewer labels
choices.why: All recipes get the same label budget.

quiz.prompt: A policy completes 10 of 10 perturbed trials of one fixed section. What can you conclude?

choices.text: It handled that section and its small perturbations; the success rate over other tracks and starts is still uncertain
choices.why: Trials inside one section are not independent draws from the whole track population.

choices.text: It is 100% reliable
choices.why: Ten correlated trials of one section cannot establish that.

choices.text: Its 95% interval is 100% to 100%
choices.why: A Wilson interval would assume ten independent random starts.

quiz.prompt: Why does the lab train every recipe with ten seeds?

choices.text: Seed-to-seed variation can be as large as the difference between recipes
choices.why: Identical recipes differ by many sections across seeds in the reference results.

choices.text: To make training run faster
choices.why: More seeds take longer.

choices.text: One seed is enough if the loss curve is smooth
choices.why: A smooth loss does not reveal closed-loop variability.

quiz.prompt: Retraining without the heading inputs barely changes success. The safest conclusion is

choices.text: Other inputs, such as the road previews, may carry the same information, so heading's importance is unproven
choices.why: An input-removal experiment cannot separate information that is encoded twice.

choices.text: Heading is useless for driving
choices.why: Heading is physically essential; the network may recover it from other inputs.

choices.text: The experiment must be invalid
choices.why: The experiment is valid; the interpretation needs care.

quiz.prompt: From the car's state at 4.0 s the expert can still finish the section, yet the learner crashed at 7.0 s. What does this show?

choices.text: The situation was recoverable by the expert at 4.0 s; the damage happened afterwards, though this does not identify one cause
choices.why: The test is a counterfactual about a state, not a proof of causation.

choices.text: The final steering command caused the crash
choices.why: The expert-recovery test points earlier than the crash.

choices.text: The expert is perfect
choices.why: A success from one state says nothing about every state.

quiz.prompt: Why freeze the model before looking at the sealed test circuits?

choices.text: Any choice influenced by test results turns the test into a tuning set
choices.why: After exposure, further results are exploratory.

choices.text: Tuning on a test set is fine if no weights are copied
choices.why: Selection by test score leaks just as training does.

choices.text: To save time
choices.why: Freezing is about validity, not speed.

quiz.prompt: A driver trained without noise is evaluated under sensor noise. This

choices.text: Measures robustness to a shift it never trained for; it does not make the driver robust
choices.why: Learning robustness would require training under noise and then measuring again.

choices.text: Makes the driver robust to noise
choices.why: Evaluation changes nothing in the weights.

choices.text: Proves it is safe in a real car
choices.why: This is a toy simulator with ideal previews.

quiz.prompt: Which is the best hypothesis for a worksheet?

choices.text: Raising weight decay from 0 to 0.1 lowers validation loss but does not raise closed-loop success
choices.why: One factor, two measurable outcomes, stated before running.

choices.text: Training will work better
choices.why: Not measurable and no factor is named.

choices.text: Everything improves with more settings changed at once
choices.why: Changing several factors makes the cause impossible to isolate.

quiz.prompt: A rule-based controller fails every recovery section but completes most nominal ones. How should the comparison with a neural policy be reported?

choices.text: Report completed sections separately for nominal and recovery starts, never averaged into one number
choices.why: A single average hides which situations each controller handles.

choices.text: Report only the progress percentage
choices.why: A short failed run has high progress per second but no completed section.

choices.text: Report only the best run
choices.why: Best-of selection overstates reliability.

quiz.prompt: An imitation learner and a reinforcement learner are each trained to drive the same circuit. What is each one given to learn from?

choices.text: Imitation: the expert's steering and speed for the states it visits. Reinforcement: only a reward score for what it does, from experience it generates itself
choices.why: What is supplied is what separates the two methods; the network and the car are the same.

choices.text: Both are given the expert's steering for every state; reinforcement just trains for longer
choices.why: Reinforcement has no labels at all. It sees only the reward, so it has to discover good steering by trying things.

choices.text: Imitation is given a reward and reinforcement is given labels
choices.why: The other way round: labels belong to imitation, a reward to reinforcement.

quiz.prompt: In module 12 both cars complete the lap. What does comparing how they were trained show?

choices.text: Reinforcement needed many times more driving steps before its car stayed on the lap, but it needed no expert to label any of them
choices.why: The costs differ in kind: labels from an expert for imitation, a great deal of simulated experience for reinforcement.

choices.text: Reinforcement needed fewer steps because it explores for itself
choices.why: Searching with only a reward is slow; an expert's label carries far more information per step.

choices.text: Both needed about the same number of steps because they train the same network
choices.why: The network is the same, but the information each driving step carries is not.

quiz.prompt: A reinforcement car completes the lap, but its steering angle flips direction every 0.1 s. Its reward paid for distance and penalised crashing only. Which explanation fits best?

choices.text: Nothing in the reward penalised flicking the steering, and flicking did not slow the lap, so nothing pushed the car to stop
choices.why: The learner optimises exactly the reward it is given; behaviour the reward ignores is left to chance.

choices.text: The algorithm has a bug: a correct reinforcement learner always drives smoothly
choices.why: The algorithm did what it was asked. The reward left smoothness out, so smoothness was never asked for.

choices.text: It will smooth out with more training
choices.why: More training makes the car better at the reward as written, flicking included.

quiz.prompt: A car completes the lap at stage 3, fails at stages 4 and 5, then completes it at every stage from 6 onward. What should you report?

choices.text: The car stays on the lap from stage 6; stage 3 showed it could lap but not that it was reliable, and several seeds would show how typical that is
choices.why: A stage counts as learned when it and every later stage lap; the early success is evidence of ability, not of reliability.

choices.text: It learned the lap at stage 3, and the later failures are noise
choices.why: One success is not reliability, and the failures that followed are evidence too.

choices.text: Report the stage-3 lap time, because it was the best result
choices.why: Reporting the best or first success overstates reliability.

modules.title: Predict before moving
discussion: Does changing speed alone change the steering command? Why might it?
Which outputs are learned and which are produced by fixed controllers?

modules.title: Build a dataset and train
discussion: Why is a validation drive different from shuffled frames?
What does the stress curve measure that validation does not?
When the success curve falls while the loss falls, what did training optimise?

modules.title: One training step
discussion: Why can the loss rise on a single step?
Why does the finite-difference check agree with backpropagation?

modules.title: Rules versus learning
discussion: Why is the section, not the trial, the unit of replication?
What does a failed run's progress percentage mean?

modules.title: Remove inputs and retrain
discussion: Which comparisons survive seed-to-seed variation?
Which removed inputs are still encoded elsewhere?

modules.title: Training playground
discussion: When does a larger network stop helping?
What do weight decay and early stopping change in the curves?
Do linear and nearest-neighbour baselines drive?

modules.title: Data coverage and DAgger
discussion: Which recipe visits states its data never covered?
What does the staged expert-only control isolate?
How do failed collections and rejected starts change what the budgets mean?

modules.title: Diagnose a failure
discussion: Where does the learner first disagree with the expert, and did it matter?
Why might permutation importance credit the wrong input?

modules.title: Generalization and leakage
discussion: What counts as exposure?
Why is a score on contaminated labels not an unseen-test result?

modules.title: Robustness challenges
discussion: Which shift causes the largest drop, and why does grip fail so abruptly in this toy model?
How would you train for robustness and then check it?

modules.title: Guided experiments
discussion: Which of your hypotheses did the data contradict?
What would a better experiment control?

modules.title: From zero to a lap: imitation versus reinforcement
discussion: Both learners start with a car that cannot drive. What did each need to be given before it could improve, and what did that cost?
Find the first picture in each row where the car completes a lap. Does the next picture also complete it? What does that say about trusting one good run?

Choose the reward without the steering-smoothness term and train again. Whose fault is the flicking steering: the algorithm's or the reward's? How would you notice a problem like this in a real project?
Which learner would you choose if you had no expert? If simulated crashes were free? If every real crash cost money?

criteria.name: Hypothesis
descriptors: Not stated, or stated after the result.
Stated, but vague or without a measurable outcome.
Stated before running, names one factor and a measurable outcome.
As proficient, with a reasoned expected direction and size.

criteria.name: Controlled design
descriptors: Several factors changed at once.
One factor changed, but starts, seeds or budgets differ between conditions.
One factor changed with matched starts, seeds and budgets.
As proficient, with a control or ablation that isolates the mechanism.

criteria.name: Evidence and statistics
descriptors: Single run or a pooled count with no uncertainty.
Several runs, but the wrong unit of replication or a misapplied interval.
Seeds or sections used as the unit, with an interval or range and per-section counts.
As proficient, with paired comparisons and a statement of what the interval does not cover.

criteria.name: Interpretation and limits
descriptors: Claims a general result from a small or exploratory sample.
Conclusion matches the numbers but ignores limitations.
Conclusion is qualified by sample size, exploratory status and simulator limits.
As proficient, and proposes a follow-up experiment that could contradict it.

criteria.name: Reproducibility
descriptors: Settings and seeds not recorded.
Some settings recorded.
Settings, seeds, model fingerprint and exposure flags exported.
As proficient, and another student reproduces the key number from the export.

worksheets.title: Predict steering
worksheets.prompt: Pick one input and sweep it over three values. Predict the direction and size of the steering command and whether the controller brakes, then run the sweep. Does a correct guess prove you understand the network?

worksheets.title: Label quality
worksheets.prompt: Corrupt a share of the steering labels, retrain from scratch for several seeds and compare validation loss (clean labels) with closed-loop success. What would wrong labels teach?

worksheets.title: Gradient mechanics
worksheets.prompt: Compare backpropagated gradients with finite differences for random parameters, and compare one Adam step with a plain gradient step. Explain the sign of a gradient and why the two steps differ.

worksheets.title: Rules and learning
worksheets.prompt: Keep the starts fixed and compare the rule, the expert and your neural policy over a pool of sections. Report nominal and recovery sections separately.

worksheets.title: Feature information
worksheets.prompt: Retrain matched input variants over several seeds. Which differences survive the seed spread? Which removed inputs are still encoded elsewhere?

worksheets.title: Capacity and overfitting
worksheets.prompt: Train three network sizes on a small dataset. Predict which size overfits most, then compare train, validation and closed-loop results over seeds.

worksheets.title: Coverage and DAgger
worksheets.prompt: Run the data-strategy experiment. Predict which recipe covers recoveries best, then compare per-seed outcomes and the data-support measures. What does the staged control show?

worksheets.title: Failure diagnosis
worksheets.prompt: Record a failed drive, find where it first departs from the expert and run the expert-recovery test. Where did the damage happen, and what can you not conclude?

worksheets.title: Generalization integrity
worksheets.prompt: Freeze a model, then reveal the sealed circuits once. Record the fingerprint and exposure flags and explain why a later score would be exploratory.

worksheets.title: Robustness
worksheets.prompt: Change one of noise, delay or grip over three values with the same paired seeds and sections. Interpret the intervals and the paired differences.

worksheets.title: Safety trade-offs
worksheets.prompt: Measure completed sections, wall contacts and minimum clearance separately. Can completion improve while clearance shrinks?

worksheets.title: Imitation versus reinforcement
worksheets.prompt: Predict how many driving steps each learner needs before its car completes the lap and stays on it. Train both on one circuit for several seeds, then compare the medians, the final lap times and how many final cars flick the steering. Which prediction did the numbers contradict? (About a minute per seed.)

setup: Double-click index.html. No server, account or network is needed; nothing is uploaded.
Every browser keeps its own session. Students download a results card (no names, no free text) and hand it in; class_dashboard.html aggregates the cards locally.

The sealed circuits are a classroom protocol, not secrecy: the page embeds them. For blind claims generate a fresh teacher-controlled test pack with tools/make_fresh_pack.py and give it to students only after they freeze their recipes.
limits: The expert is a heuristic: about 2% of fast typical starts trip the lateral-acceleration limit within the first steps.
Apex Park and Square Sprint contain small inner-wall loops at their tightest bends; they are excluded from the monitor and headline pools and flagged in the track list.
Grip scales the lateral-acceleration limit and braking; it is a hard threshold, not a tyre-slip model.
Noise perturbs lane, heading and speed; the road previews stay ideal.

Module 12's reinforcement learner is a small PPO written for this lab. A training run takes about a minute of browser time, so the worksheet uses three seeds by default; the saved reference run (every circuit, ten seeds) takes about eight minutes on twelve cores.

Both module 12 learners are tested on the circuit they trained on; transfer to unseen circuits is module 9's question, and the imitation-versus-reinforcement comparison is of cost in this simulator, not a ranking of the two families.
